title: Beijing's Pressure On Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) Fails To Shake The Bull Case - londoninsider.co.uk
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE: TSM) finds itself at the centre of a growing geopolitical storm as Beijing escalates pressure on the island nation it claims as its own territory. China has long regarded Taiwan as a breakaway province, and its increasingly assertive military and diplomatic posturing has placed TSM squarely in the crosshairs of global investor anxiety. TSM is the world’s most advanced chipmaker, producing the semiconductors that power everything from smartphones to artificial intelligence data centres and modern defence systems. The company manufactures chips for virtually every major technology firm on the planet, giving it an almost irreplaceable role in the global technology supply chain. Beijing’s targeting of Taiwan is not merely a political matter, but a direct challenge to the stability of an industry that underpins trillions of dollars in global economic output each year. Any disruption to TSM’s operations, whether through military conflict, economic coercion, or forced decoupling, would send shockwaves through technology markets worldwide and across virtually every sector that relies on advanced chips. Despite the elevated risk profile, the bull case for TSM remains structurally compelling given the company’s unrivalled manufacturing capabilities and its dominance in leading-edge chip production. No competitor, including Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) or Samsung, has been able to meaningfully close the technology gap that TSM has built up over decades of focused investment and engineering excellence. The global demand for advanced semiconductors continues to accelerate, driven by the explosive growth of artificial intelligence workloads, cloud computing infrastructure, and next-generation consumer electronics. TSM’s expansion into new geographies, including its Arizona fabrication plants in the United States and facilities in Japan, is helping reduce the concentration risk that has historically concerned investors focused on cross-strait tensions. The United States government has actively supported TSM’s overseas expansion through the CHIPS Act, recognising that securing access to advanced semiconductor manufacturing is a matter of national security. This geopolitical backing from Washington provides TSM with a layer of protection and strategic importance that purely commercial competitors cannot easily replicate or undermine. Investors weighing the risks must balance the very real threat posed by Beijing’s ambitions against the equally real difficulty any aggressor would face in replacing what TSM produces for the world. The bull case, in short, rests on the argument that TSM is too critical to the global economy for markets to price it as though disruption were either imminent or survivable without severe consequences for all parties involved. title: Hormel SPAM Shows Up In Two New Kwik Trip Breakfast Sandwiches - 98.1 - Minnesota's New Country
content: Kwik Trip just rolled out two new breakfast sandwiches, and they are very Minnesotan. Kwik Trip went all in with their latest creations, inviting Hormel's SPAM to the breakfast table. If you are a fan of the infamous canned meat, you're likely to try one. The breakfast sandwiches rolled out this morning, and I had to try one, as I am a big fan of SPAM. I ended up getting the classic brunch sandwich, which has SPAM, egg, and cheese on a croissant. It's similar to the sausage or bacon croissant, but it substitutes SPAM for the other familiar breakfast meats. The SPAM looked to be pre-sliced and was about a quarter of an inch thick on my sandwich. Overall, to me, it was good. Other than the slightly saltier flavor, it was as enjoyable as the other breakfast options. Sign up for the 98.1 Minnesota's New Country Newsletter The second option was the Western Omelette breakfast sandwich option. That sandwich features SPAM, the Kwik Trip Western Omelette, and cheese on a hamburger bun. Both sandwiches were available at the Kwik Trip off Highway 10, but I didn't get the chance to stop at other stores this morning. I am guessing that whatever Kwik Trip you stop at, the sandwiches will be there. When I told my co-workers I was running to grab a breakfast sandwich, they all were interested until I told them what I was getting. I didn't realize that SPAM was so polarizing! title: Beijing Just Aimed at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (NYSE:TSM). Here’s Why the Bull Case Still Wins - Yahoo Finance
content: Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results On July 21, the Financial Times reported that China's Ministry of Commerce is considering implementing export controls that would bar Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM) and QUALCOMM Incorporated (NASDAQ:QCOM) from manufacturing chips based on designs from Huawei, Alibaba, and ByteDance. Such headlines are likely to hit a foundry stock hard. In the case of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM), however, the Bull case remains strong as always. Here's the how and why. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM)'s Q2 net profit went up 77% year-over-year, reaching a record high of T$706.6 billion ($22 billion). Beating the consensus estimates, the increase marks the ninth straight quarter of double-digit growth. Revenue climbed 36% to NT$1.27 trillion. The company has also raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance above 40% in U.S. dollar terms in addition to lifting the 2026 capex toward $62 billion. With another $100 billion onto its U.S. build-out, the company pushes its total American commitments to $265 billion. Days later, Reuters and Bloomberg confirmed that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM) has finalized hikes in base prices between 5%-10% across advanced and mature nodes starting in 2027. The company has been the primary chipmaker for two of the largest players in the global tech market: Apple and Nvidia. Such a foundry can't freely raise prices unless it has leverage that can't be replaced. That leverage is technical as well as contractual. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited's (NYSE:TSM) N2 (2nm-class) process uses gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors, and they are roughly two to three generations ahead of China's largest semiconductor foundry, SMIC's 7nm ceiling. While achieving this feat, the company actively phased out Chinese-made equipment from its 2nm production lines to comply with U.S. regulations and relied on suppliers from the U.S., Europe, and Japan for its leading-edge manufacturing. At the moment, the Beijing proposal is not finalized. Neither Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM), QUALCOMM Incorporated (NASDAQ:QCOM), nor Beijing has confirmed the scope of this proposal, but the signal still matters. In addition to the existing Taiwan Strait risk, where potential military conflict threatens global commerce, China is willing to weaponize the foreign foundries' access to its AI and semiconductor technologies. On the other hand, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM) has a trailing P/E in the range of 27x to 36x that sits above the company's own ten-year average. Such a decade-high multiple leaves less room for error if the Beijing proposal translates to a policy. The signal doesn't stop there. On July 21, the same day Beijing reported its proposal, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM)'s VP Bor-Zen Tien made a discretionary, open-market purchase of the company's shares and ADSs outside the company's scheduled Employee Stock Purchase Plan. The insider purchase, amounting to just $301,350, modestly represents the executive's interest in the stock's growth. Meanwhile, the institutional interest in the stock materially reflects the market expectations. Insider Monkey's database shows 234 hedge funds holding ownership stakes in Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE:TSM), as of Q1 2026, up from 224 a quarter earlier, with the dollar value of those stakes reaching $39.2 billion. Short interest sits at just 0.57% of float, indicating that very few investors are betting against the stock. Beijing's proposal is a potential tailwind, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited's (NYSE:TSM) premium multiple means the market has little patience for one going wrong. But the remaining evidence, including the record earnings, pricing power over the largest customers, a product lead almost without the involvement of China, growing hedge fund conviction, and near-zero short interest, points strongly to a bull case, capable of surviving a headline. title: TSMC Raises 2026 CapEx Budget to Capture Long-Term AI, HPC Demand - TradingView
content: In the second quarter of 2026,Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company TSM, or TSMC, generated nearly New Taiwan Dollar (“TWD”) 783 billion in cash from operations, spent TWD 496 billion in capital expenditure and distributed TWD 156 billion as its third-quarter 2025 cash dividend. Even so, the company’s cash balance increased TWD 99 billion to TWD 3.1 trillion at the end of the quarter. TSMC views higher capital spending as a reflection of greater growth opportunities over the coming years. Backed by its strong technology leadership and differentiation, the company believes it is well-positioned to capture the multiyear structural demand from the industry megatrends of 5G, artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC). Citing strong structural demand from customers, including the emerging Agentic AI market, TSMC raised its full-year 2026 capital budget to be between $60 billion and $64 billion. The company works closely with the tool equipment suppliers well ahead of time to prepare capacity, whether it is a strong up cycle or down cycle. Likewise, customers collaborate with the company well in advance to plan their capacity needs. As such, TSMC does not expect any bottlenecks to its capacity expansion plans. Of the total capital budget, roughly 70% to 80% will be allocated to TSMC’s advanced process technologies, about 10% to specialty technologies and 10%-20% to advanced packaging, testing, mask-making and other areas. Even as it continues to invest heavily in 2026, TSMC reiterated its commitment to delivering profitable growth for shareholders. GlobalFoundries Inc. GFS generated $542 million in cash flow from operations in the first quarter of 2026. Capital expenditure, net of proceeds from government grants, was $309 million or roughly 19% of revenues. The company is expanding capacity in high-growth technology corridors such as silicon photonics, FDX and high-performance SiGe to unlock sustainable accretive revenue growth. GlobalFoundries expects net capital expenditure to increase in the second quarter, driven by the timing of tool delivery windows and government grants. GFS also reaffirmed its full-year 2026 non-IFRS net capital expenditure outlook of 15%-20% of revenues. United Microelectronics Corp. UMC reported NT$21.98 billion in operating cash flows in the first quarter of 2026. Cash outflow from investing activities totaled NT$21.35 billion, including NT$13.16 billion in capital expenditures, resulting in free cash flow of NT$8.83 billion. UMC reiterated its overall annual capital expenditure budget to be roughly $1.5 billionduring the April earnings call. TSM currently trades at a forward, five-year Price/Sales (P/S) of 10.86X, above its historical median of 8.12X while remaining in line with the industry average. title: Forget Picking the Next AI Winner: TSM Lets You Profit From Every Wave of the Revolution - AOL.com
content:
TSM posted $40 billion in Q2 revenue, up 39% year over year, with EPS climbing 61% as AI demand continues to outstrip manufacturing supply. CEO C.C. Wei says agentic AI is reviving CPU demand in data centers, and every major architecture runs through TSMC's fabs, including x86, ARM, and RISC-V. TSM manufactures chips for Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Broadcom, and Qualcomm, giving investors AI exposure without betting on which single designer wins. Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today. Artificial intelligence is moving into a new phase. The first wave centered on building massive GPU clusters to train ever-larger models. Now the industry is broadening. Companies are investing in AI memory, networking, storage, and increasingly powerful CPUs to support emerging workloads such as agentic AI. That shift matters because it expands the number of semiconductor companies benefiting from AI spending instead of narrowing it. Few businesses are better positioned to capitalize on that trend than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM), which manufactures chips for nearly every major AI designer regardless of which technology ultimately comes out on top. Taiwan Semiconductor's second-quarter results underscored just how central the company has become to the AI ecosystem. According to its second-quarter earnings release, revenue climbed to NT$1.27 trillion (about $40 billion), up 36% year over year, while net income surged 77%. The stock listed in Taiwan climbed 2.6% over the week. The key figure is 3%. TSMC’s 2-nanometer process accounted for 3% of wafer revenue in the second quarter. The company projects the process ramp will reduce gross margin by three to four points in the second half. The disparity sheds light on the stock’s turnaround. The ADR surged 5.6% on Tuesday following news of price increases for 2027, but then dropped 5.0% by Friday. According to two sources who spoke with Reuters, TSMC intends to raise prices by as much as 10%. The adjustments are expected to address costs for materials, equipment, and construction of overseas fabrication plants. TSMC would not comment on exact pricing. The company described its pricing strategy as “strategic, not opportunistic.” Reuters Third-quarter numbers represent the midpoint of the company’s outlook. Share price changes reflect unadjusted closing values. The table outlines the investor trade-off. TSMC anticipates another significant increase in sales. Despite this growth, profitability is projected to decline. Revenue for the third quarter is projected at $44.6 billion to $45.8 billion, marking sequential growth of roughly 12% at the midpoint. Gross margin is expected in the range of 65% to 67%. The ramp-up of 2nm technology is a key source of pressure. Additional headwinds come from overseas facilities. TSMC anticipates an initial overseas-fab margin dilution of two to three points, potentially increasing to three to four points over time. TSMC increased its capital budget for 2026 to a range of $60 billion to $64 billion, with around 70%-80% allocated for advanced-process technologies. The company’s management continues to anticipate full-year revenue in dollar terms to rise a bit above 40%. The company’s core operations stayed robust. Net income for the second quarter rose 77.4% to NT$706.56 billion. Advanced technologies accounted for 77% of wafer revenue. Overall, the data suggest the announced pricing strategy has a defensive tone. Raising prices may help safeguard profits as capital spending rises. Wei emphasized customer stability rather than sudden growth. “I don’t want to squeeze them out from the market,” he said. Wei added that TSMC depends on its customers’ ongoing success. League Classic is getting closer to release, and Riot Games is hosting showmatches around the world to get fans excited about the mode. We sat down with Jake Kevin “Xmithie” Puchero after his victory in the LCS League Classic TSM VS CLG showmatch to discuss his thoughts on the game mode, the biggest differences compared to modern League, why new players should jump into Classic, and why he stopped being a head coach. It was definitely nostalgic. It was fun, but at the same time, not exactly enjoyable as a jungler in that era. Luca: It looked really hard to clear camps in League Classic, from what I saw. I’ve never played it myself, but a lot of people are complaining about how strong the camps were. It has been a long time since you were last on stage, and you were coaching at the time. When you play competitively, you get that adrenaline from stepping on stage, and I don’t know if that’s something players actually miss after retiring. Xmithie: Honestly, it didn’t feel that different. I’m so used to being on stage that it felt pretty natural. I was much more comfortable than anxious or full of adrenaline, especially because I’ve been with my teammates, Eugene, Pobelter, Doublelift, and Darshan for such a long time. It just felt very natural to me. Luca: Doublelift actually had a different reaction from you, because he seemed to really enjoy playing the role. You didn’t, as you said, and you got put on Skarner, which is one of your signature picks. I don’t know if you had the chance to look at the new Skarner compared to the old one, the one with the ultimate. Xmithie: The new Skarner is definitely much more fun. You can go through walls, you can ult more than one person, and it’s not just a point-and-click ability. There’s much more utility, and a lot more ways to outplay with Skarner. There are so many combos you can do now, compared to the old version, where you basically just pressed R. Luca: You were forced to play jungle, but there’s a lot of fun stuff in Classic. Xmithie: Skarner is really broken, which is why he was probably perma-banned in pretty much every game. Neither jungler could really play him. But I think mid lane is definitely the most broken role in this meta, because you have Sion, Master Yi, Kassadin, those three champions stand out, but honestly, everything else is really broken too. So I’d definitely say mid is the favorite role. Jungle is also really favorable for camping mid, since camps respawn every 45 seconds. There’s not really a jungle route in this meta, it’s literally just take one camp, gank mid, take one camp, and then race. It’s pretty linear. Xmithie: More recently, I started watching a lot more. Before that, I mainly watched my friends play. We’re good friends with Huhi and Impact, so I would mostly just watch Sentinels games, and that was pretty much it. Luca: The atmosphere between how League used to be back in the day and how it is now feels quite different. It seems like something is missing, because the fan support isn’t the same and the venues aren’t as full as they used to be. Xmithie: These events are really good for the game. They’re healthy because they bring back that nostalgic feeling. Especially now that League Classic is coming back, more old players are trying to get back in, and I think it’s one of the ways to bring more players back into the game. Luca: So we’re focusing a lot on nostalgia for older players, but there’s another point here. Xmithie: For me personally, I didn’t actually play at the very beginning of League. I didn’t play Season 1 or the start of Season 2; I came in at the end of Season 2. I also didn’t play jungle back then; I played mid and top. When this came out, I was basically only playing Lee Sin and Jarvan as jungle champions. I didn’t really play anything else, so a lot of it felt new to me. I think that would be true for new players, too. Even though it’s a classic game, there are still a lot of new things, and a lot of old things that are even more broken now than they are today. So I think new players can definitely try it out. Xmithie: It brings back good memories, so it’s definitely fun. Luca: Doublelift told me that you were basically tryharding the whole game because of the rivalry between CLG and TSM. Xmithie: I think it was a content game for Doublelift, because he got caught four or five times that game. He was too focused on trying to carry on Vayne, so he tried to 1v9, but obviously, it didn’t go well for him. Luca: You played for many years, and you also tried coaching. There’s a topic going around in the League scene right now, because a lot of pro players are becoming coaches, and it’s also starting to happen in VALORANT. You tried coaching with Immortals and then you stopped. Xmithie: The reason I stopped was a combination of a few things. At the time, I felt like I needed to do something different or decide whether I wanted to stay on that path. I was also thinking about whether I wanted to go back to school or keep coaching. And if I kept coaching, would it be consistent? Would salaries go down? Or would I just end up in a stagnant situation? There were a lot of scenarios going through my head about what I should do, but in the end, I felt coaching wasn’t really a long-term investment for me, so I decided to stop and look for other career paths. I definitely think League is better now. It’s more balanced. Xmithie: Back then, it required a different kind of skill. I only realized that later, because you had to conserve mana. League Classic is getting closer to release, and Riot Games is hosting showmatches around the world to get fans excited about the mode. We sat down with Peng “Doublelift” Yi-Liang after his victory in the LCS League Classic showmatch between TSM and CLG to discuss his thoughts on the game mode, the biggest differences compared to modern League, why new players should jump into Classic, and his future plans for creating content around it. Doublelift: I think the first one was a little cooler in terms of the venue because there were so many people, but the second one was more nostalgic for me because it was CLG vs TSM, and that’s something I lived through. I’d say they’re kind of tied. That’s a bit of a cop out answer, but I really enjoyed both. Luca: In terms of gameplay, Riot made some adjustments between the two matches. Doublelift: I actually did not notice much difference. The champs are the same and they did not really add or remove any. The biggest difference was just how different the vibes were. In the first showmatch, everyone was not taking it that seriously, and I had to be the guy saying, ‘Maybe we should try to win this, you know?’ But in this one, it was TSM vs CLG, so there was already a bit of rivalry there, and my team came out of the gate really wanting to win. We were immediately thinking about the most OP team comps, the most OP champs, and the best builds. So I think the level of seriousness was a lot higher in this one for pretty obvious reasons. Doublelift: Yeah. It was kind of a content game, but I did not think Kassadin was that broken, actually. We did not really understand what was that OP yet, and then in game three, we were back to tryharding. Doublelift: I mean, it is all mid champs. It has to be Gragas, AP Yi, and Kassadin; absolutely 100 percent. Also, the game is so imbalanced. Range supports are just so broken compared to melee supports. I think that is the whole point of it. It is really imbalanced. I thought about it and asked myself, why not just go back and balance it so Kassadin is not as OP and all that? But I think the whole point people want to experience again is the janky and crazy stuff that you could play back then. I would say the most OP stuff is usually mid lane champions, and then for bot lane it is range supports plus Vayne or Corki. They are just so strong. Luca: Everything looked so goofy in terms of the game, and it was really fun to watch from the outside. But as players, you all looked like you were enjoying yourselves too, everyone had smiles on their faces. Doublelift: Yeah, I think fun stuff like this has definitely been missing. There is a limit to it, right? If every single week or every single month there was some sort of fun showmatch like this, people would naturally get tired of it. That is how it goes with anything that gets done too much. But there was nothing like this for so many years that I think people were basically starving for showmatches, rivalry matches, nostalgia matches, and stuff like that. League of Legends was pretty perfect for it. It is an important time for a lot of us pros, but also for a lot of people who played back then. It was the time when you first got into the game, and it looked and played really differently. The feelings you had about it were still special, though. It is cool to see it and think, ‘Oh, I remember that, this was so OP.’ You just get to go back down that path and revisit those memories. This stuff is awesome. It has been received really well. The community loves it, and everyone who is playing seems to love it, too. So I hope they do more stuff like this in the future, but they do it tastefully, so they are not milking it too hard. Luca: You were speaking about remembering things, but I actually do not remember anything because I never watched any classic game and I never had the chance to play it. That is what it is. It is a very old game design. It was basically just, let us do it like this, and almost nothing makes sense. Items cost really random amounts. They can range from 2000 gold to 4000 gold. Modern League has a lot more systems. There are more systems around items, waves, plates, and all of that. But when you play old League, it is all about the champions and the items you are playing. That is literally the only thing that matters. Baron is not that important. Drake is not that important. Gold is not that important. It is just who has the most OP build and champion. It definitely takes me back to the kind of League I enjoyed back then, and I can compare it to modern League and see there are things I like and things I do not like. Oh, absolutely not. It was not better. The game has only gotten better since then. There are parts of it that I liked and still like, but at the end of the day, the game had to get a lot better for people to keep playing for 15 years. It had to improve. So many games have come out since then to compete with League and try to take people’s time and attention away, but people are still stuck with League because it has gotten better every single year. Luca: When we think about old League, nostalgia, and all the things that were cool or broken, new players do not really know old League. You are playing the mode because you have that nostalgia. Doublelift: I would say just come into it with an open mind. It is definitely not the same game at all, and so many things have gotten better over time. You just have to appreciate it for what it was, almost like an alternate dimension of the game you play now. Back then, the fact that you had to grind for runes and level up your account to get masteries was stupid. It did not make any sense. Why should a new player have fewer stats than someone who has grinded for rune pages and stuff? If you think the game right now is imbalanced, and a lot of people do, they hate mages, they hate how weak tanks are, they think lethality champions are broken, there are already a lot of things people complain about. But League Classic is so much more imbalanced than modern League. Riot has done a very good job of making it so the worst champion in the game is not that much worse than the best champion in the game. There is a big difference in modern League, obviously, but not that big. You can play Shyvana, Heimerdinger, and Jayce and still do well. You do not need to play meta champions all the time. In League Classic, there are broken things, okay things, and terrible things, and there is a huge gap between them. So if you come in with the mindset of experimenting and trying to figure out what is okay and what works, it makes you appreciate how much the game has changed since then. I would love to do something like that. One thing that would actually be pretty funny would be to bring in new generation players who have never played it, we classic players grew up with the game. But I think what is funnier is bringing in players who only came in recently and have never played League Classic, then making them go back, play it, and figure it out. That has not been done before. I have a bunch of ideas for tournaments we could do with Classic or otherwise that could be really cool. No comments yet. Be the first one to start the discussion. You must log in to leave a comment. title: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), And TSMC (NYSE: TSM) Stand To Gain Most If AI Spending Reaches $1 Trillion - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By David Prior | Jul 24, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Global AI infrastructure investment is accelerating at a pace that few analysts fully anticipated, with hyperscaler capital expenditure projections rising steadily throughout 2026. The four major AI hyperscalers are collectively on track to spend around $650 billion on data center capital expenditures this year, a figure that is already staggering by historical standards. Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has projected that total AI spending could reach $1 trillion in 2027, a forecast that aligns with signals already coming from major players in the space. Alphabet told investors during its Q1 2026 conference call to expect “significantly” higher capital expenditures in 2027, telegraphing an unusually large spending increase well ahead of schedule. Three companies are best positioned to capture the bulk of that windfall: Nvidia, Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM). Nvidia remains the dominant force in AI infrastructure, with its GPUs establishing themselves as the industry standard for data center computing power across a wide range of tasks. Last quarter, Nvidia posted revenue growth of 85%, with next quarter’s revenue expected to nearly double year over year, yet the stock trades at just 22 times forward earnings. Broadcom is carving out its own space in the AI chip market by partnering directly with hyperscalers to design custom application-specific integrated circuits purpose-built for narrow workloads. These custom chips are far more cost-effective than GPUs for the specific tasks they handle, and Broadcom expects to generate $100 billion or more in AI semiconductor revenue during 2027 alone. For context, Broadcom generated $75 billion in total revenue over the past 12 months, meaning AI chip sales alone could exceed the company’s entire recent annual revenue base. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing operates differently from Nvidia and Broadcom, functioning as a chip manufacturer rather than a designer competing for data center market share. TSMC benefits regardless of which chip designer wins the AI race, since it manufactures chips for both Nvidia and Broadcom, meaning rising demand across the board drives its growth. TSMC CEO C.C. Wei stated during the company’s most recent conference call that he sees chip demand staying strong through at least 2029 to 2030, citing the AI build-out as having created an entirely new industry segment. That long-term visibility makes TSMC a compelling investment not just for the remainder of this year, but across the broader arc of this decade’s AI-driven infrastructure expansion. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.
